answer: HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded): In this dataset, Black students do NOT post an actual completion-rate advantage at any SES level — their BA-completion rate is lower than White (and pooled-other) rates at every global-SES level and never crosses over. The honest pattern is the inverse: the White-minus-Black completion gap is SMALLEST at the highest socioeconomic levels. Across global-SES terciles the White−Black gap narrows monotonically from 2.61 pp (low) to 1.67 pp (mid) to 1.59 pp (high); across quartiles it is smallest in the top quartile (0.64 pp; Q1 1.34, Q2 2.99, Q3 2.10 pp). Equivalently, Black completion rates rise fastest with SES — Black rises from ~0.44% (lowest tercile/quartile) to 2.22–3.03% at the top, while White rates stay roughly flat (3.05→3.81% terciles; 1.78→3.67% quartiles). The continuous-SES logistic model confirms this: SES×Black interaction β=+0.76 (p=0.003), joint race×SES interaction LR χ²=9.57 (p=0.008), with the predicted Black−White difference compressing from −2.24 pp at the 10th SES centile to −0.84 pp at the 90th. So the advantage framing holds only in the sense that Black students' completion-rate deficit vs. White/others is least pronounced at HIGH SES; it never becomes a true advantage, and even the narrowed top-quartile gap rests on very few events (Black top-quartile cells: 8–9 completions, CI widths up to ~4.3 pp).

payload.hypothesis: At HIGH socioeconomic levels is the Black students' completion-rate deficit (relative to White and other students) least pronounced / the White-minus-Black completion gap smallest, though it never becomes an actual Black advantage.
payload.workflow: 1) Bucketed SES into global terciles and quartiles; computed P(BA=1) per race x SES level with n, event counts, Wilson 95% CI widths. 2) Defined the comparison as the gap in percentage points: White-minus-Black, pooled-other-minus-Black, Hispanic-minus-Black at each SES level. 3) Tested significance via logistic regression P(BA) ~ continuous SES x race (baseline White) with an LR test on the interaction terms. 4) Sensitivity: terciles vs quartiles vs continuous interaction; White vs pooled-other baselines; a model adjusted for ability (ASVAB composite) and class percentile (interpretation only); and within-race SES terciles as a secondary lens (flagged as unequal absolute SES). 5) All headline claims are descriptive, with the significant interaction reported explicitly and sparsity (236 events, single-digit Black top-SES cells) kept visible.
